To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cross border patient mobility might reduce health care quality when patients are heterogeneous in income.
cross border patient mobility has ambiguous effects on quality, welfare and health expenditures in low and middle income regions and no effect on quality and welfare in the high-income region.

(i) cross border mobility of patients is likely to be welfare reducing for the regions that lose patients and welfare improving for the regions that attract patients; (ii) the effect on welfare is ambiguous in the regions that neither gain nor lose patients; and (iii), the effects of cross-border mobility are more likely to be welfare improving for regions with higher income and welfare reducing for regions with lower income.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a policy dilemma: the welfare gains from patient mobility can be outweighed by quality losses.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effect of cross border patient flow on health care quality is ambiguous, but that welfare effects are unambiguous.
the welfare effect of cross border patient flows is ambiguous.
the welfare effects of cross border mobility are ambiguous and depend crucially on how income varies across regions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of patient mobility depend on the income of regions and patients.
health policies need to take into account the income distribution in the population.
